newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vranitzky to urge EU, OSCE members to help Albania.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky to urge EU, OSCE members to help Albania.

text.p: European mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Friday he will urge the European Union and OSCE member states to consider sending military support to Albania to end spreading chaos and anarchy.

Vranitzky, speaking to Reuters in Vienna by telephone from the Italian frigate Aliseo in the Adriatic where he was holding talks with Albanian government leaders, said he believed order could only be restored in Albania with outside help.
"I think order can only be established with help from abroad," the former Austrian chancellor said.
Vranitzky said he was told by Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, Foreign Minister Arjan Starova and army chief of staff General Adem Copani that they could not cope with the situation by themselves.
"They pointed out that the Albanian crisis is not a civil war. It is chaos and anarchy and they believe they can overcome it if there is support from abroad," he added.

Vranitzky said he would speak as soon as possible to Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo of the Netherlands, which currently holds the EU presidency, and Denmark's Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, current chairman of the 54-member state Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

"I will urge them today, or at the latest tomorrow, to make a decision one way or the other," he said. "I think the OSCE and the EU countries should give it very thorough thought because this seems to be the most urgent answer the Albanians have to get, otherwise chaos and anarchy will continue."

Vranitzky said it should be made clear that the request for military or police assistance would be made to individual governments and not to any particular body such as the Western European Union, considered to be the EU's future defence arm.
He said the request to governments should be made by the Netherland's Van Mierlo or Denmark's Petersen and any force should be "a coalition of those willing" to take part.
Vranitzky was transported to the frigate by Italian helicopters from Brindisi early on Friday morning because, he said, it was too dangerous for his 10-member delegation to travel to Tirana.
The appeal for foreign help was part of a larger package of measures agreed between the OSCE and the Albanian government.

Vranitzky and his team were to meet representatives of the National Committee of Public Salvation, an umbrella grouping of rebel towns in the south, at around 4 p.m. (1500 GMT) when they will discuss the proposals.

The Albanian government also backed an OSCE idea to send in teams of monitors to help modernise the Balkan state's financial institutions, advise on drawing up a constitution and strengthen the respect of human rights and democracy.
The package was also agreed by President Sali Berisha, Vranitzky said, as well as each member of the mission, representing the United States, Russia, Denmark, the Netherlands, Greece and Italy.

Other monitors would help Albania's security forces to collect the thousands of arms seized across the country from ransacked army and police arsenals -- one of the most difficult proposals which needs the backing of town committees if it had even a slim chance of working.

Teams of OSCE observers would also closely monitor general elections, slated for June. The OSCE, which groups Europe, the United States and Canada, criticised last May's elections as seriously flawed. Berisha's rightist Democratic Party won nearly all seats in parliament.
